newsitem.title: SPAIN: Retail fuels Madrid bourse, analysts get cautious.
newsitem.headline: Retail fuels Madrid bourse, analysts get cautious.

text.p: A flow of funds from retail investors has driven the Madrid bourse to test new highs but analysts are wondering how much further it can go.
They say quoted firms are now overvalued, with the Madrid general index having already surpassed most brokers' year-end targets of around 500-525.
The index hit an all-time high of 525.85 on Monday.

Despite fresh all-time highs set recently, the bourse may well continue to gain from domestic fund flows, Mariano Colmenar of BZW brokerage said. But further gains now would only heighten the risk of correction later in the year.

"If retail investors keep buying, then of course prices will continue to rise. But for me there are few alternatives left," Colmenar said. "...The problem we have (in making bourse forecasts) is not one of valuation but of funds flow."
Stocks have primarily been driven up lately by small investors looking for value as more traditional fixed-income investments become less attractive due to a sharp decline in key interest rates.
The benchmark 10-year bond yield is now around 6.7 percent, while the key money market rate is at 5.50 percent, having fallen from 9.25 percent at the end of 1995.
Most economists see it heading down to about 5.00 percent before year-end, eyeing a continued improvement in inflation, already at its lowest level in almost 30 years.
But analysts said all these factors are already fully reflected in current prices and have been for some time.
Even when prices are high, if funds keep coming into the market there can be little chance for a correction. The impulse for a pullback could come from fresh news, BZW's Colmenar said.
For the moment, he has not changed his year-end general index target of 500-510, although this is under constant review.
The seemingly insatiable public demand for shares which has fuelled repeated record-breaking performances this year should inspire caution, some experts said.

"You know it's time to take profits when people you meet on the street ask you about which shares they should buy. You can almost take it as read that prices have reached maximums as retail buyers tend to invest badly," said one analyst who asked not to be named.
This tendency has been exacerbated by public share offerings in key companies Telefonica in February and Repsol in April, both leaving a huge amount of unsatisfied demand on the retail tranches.
A trader at Central Hispano Bolsa agreed stocks are overvalued, predicting more gains in the short term with caution taking hold later in the year.
"Short term we'll see prices still heading up, but investors will have to start being more selective as many stocks are now overpriced," she said.
There are alternatives however. Banks may be expensive, but many of them have bright prospects.
"Anything which should see growth will always be at a premium," one analyst said.
Risks to the market could come in the shape of doubts on the progress towards European economic and monetary union, with Germany's position above all coming under close scrutiny.

"The market is discounting the best of all worlds at the moment, above all the question mark hangs over Germany. We're not ruling out a hike in German interest rates in the second half," said an analyst at a foreign brokerage.
Another agreed that this would invite caution.
"There is always the risk that we get disagreeable surprises via news from abroad about EMU, and the market should start to get more cautious," he said.
Forecasts for corporate profits this year may provide more fuel for stocks, but again only in selected cases.
"Profits will be good, but not scandalously good except in the case of some banks," BZW's Colmenar said.
